explanation: Mooren ulcer occurs in two forms: a limited, unilateral, relatively indolent type in older patients, and an aggressive, bilateral, relentlessly progressive type in younger patients, so option A reverses the association. A well-recognised subset is associated with hepatitis C, and in those patients treating the underlying viral infection with interferon alfa-2b, with or without ribavirin, can produce dramatic healing of the ulcer, which makes B correct. The third stem fragment about progression toward the sclera is also wrong: sparing of the sclera is one of the features that separates Mooren ulcer from the peripheral ulcerative keratitis of systemic vasculitis, and Mooren spreads circumferentially and then centrally with an undermined leading edge.

The aim in Descemet membrane detachment is to reappose the membrane to the posterior stroma, normally achieved by descemetopexy with an air or gas bubble such as SF6 or C3F8. For a large, planar or chronic detachment that will not tamponade with gas alone, transcorneal full-thickness 10-0 monofilament nylon sutures are placed to mechanically press the membrane back, usually combined with an intracameral air or gas fill, so A is the intended answer. Silicone oil in the anterior chamber has no role here and would risk endothelial damage and pressure problems, and deliberately leaving a large bolus of viscoelastic is actively harmful because it keeps the membrane away from the stroma and causes an intraocular pressure spike.

The ESCRS multicentre endophthalmitis study demonstrated an approximately fivefold reduction in postoperative endophthalmitis with intracameral cefuroxime 1 mg in 0.1 mL given at the end of phacoemulsification, and this is the European recommendation. Perioperative topical fluoroquinolone such as levofloxacin did not show a statistically significant independent protective effect in that trial and is adjunctive at best. Vancomycin in the irrigating bottle is specifically not recommended: the delivered dose is unreliable, it promotes resistance to a last-line antistaphylococcal agent, and it has been linked to haemorrhagic occlusive retinal vasculitis.

Conjunctival intraepithelial neoplasia is by definition a dysplastic lesion of the surface epithelium, graded mild, moderate or severe according to how much of the epithelial thickness is occupied by dysplastic cells, becoming carcinoma in situ when full thickness, so dysplasia is the defining and grading characteristic. Loss of normal maturation, nuclear pleomorphism, increased mitoses and loss of goblet cells accompany it, while the epithelial basement membrane stays intact, which is what separates CIN from invasive squamous cell carcinoma. Acanthosis, hyperkeratosis seen clinically as leukoplakia, and epithelial hyperplasia are frequently present but are non-specific reactive changes that also occur in benign lesions such as pterygium or papilloma, so none of them defines the lesion.

The facial nerve emerges from the parotid gland as five main branches: temporal (frontal), zygomatic, buccal, marginal mandibular and cervical, so zygomatic is the only unambiguously correct main branch listed. The zygomaticofacial and infraorbital branches are sensory branches of the maxillary division of the trigeminal nerve, not of cranial nerve VII, which is the trap in this item. Temporal is a genuine main branch, but temporo-parietal is not the accepted anatomical name and conflates the nerve with the temporoparietal fascia, so zygomatic remains the best answer.

Rounding or blunting of the normally sharp medial canthal angle is the classic sign that the medial canthal tendon has been avulsed or disinserted, typically with a canalicular laceration or a naso-orbito-ethmoid injury, and it is usually accompanied by traumatic telecanthus and lateral displacement of the punctum. A medial wall blowout fracture on its own does not detach the tendon and presents instead with enophthalmos, orbital emphysema or restricted abduction. A tumour or an acute dacryocystitis produces a mass or an inflamed swelling below the medial canthal tendon but leaves the canthal angle itself anatomically intact.

The Branch Vein Occlusion Study set the treatment threshold for macular oedema after BRVO as visual acuity of 20/40 or worse persisting for at least 3 months, with intraretinal haemorrhage cleared enough to permit angiography and grid laser, which is exactly option A. A specific retinal thickness value, distance from the FAZ, or the presence of hard exudates were not BVOS criteria; five disc diameters of non-perfusion is the BVOS threshold for watching for neovascularisation, not for treating oedema, so D is a deliberate near-miss. In current practice anti-VEGF therapy has largely replaced grid laser as first line, but the question is asking for the classic BVOS criterion.

After a complicated cataract extraction, pseudophakic cystoid macular oedema is the commonest treatable reason for vision failing to improve once the cornea has cleared, and it is easily confirmed on macular OCT and treated with topical NSAID plus corticosteroid, escalating to sub-Tenon or intravitreal steroid. PTK addresses anterior stromal irregularity and would do nothing for an endothelial or macular problem, and would in fact induce a hyperopic shift. Cultured endothelial cell therapy is investigational rather than a standard clinical option. Repeat DSAEK is indicated only if the graft has actually failed or dislocated, which this stem does not state, so treating the macula is the intervention most likely to gain vision.
concern: The stem is truncated in this recall (age and, more importantly, the graft and corneal status are missing). The answer assumes a clear, attached graft; if the recall omitted graft failure or persistent corneal oedema, repeat DSAEK would become the answer.

explanation: A suddenly rock-hard eye with loss of the red reflex and forward movement of the lens during cataract surgery is a suprachoroidal (expulsive) haemorrhage, and the single priority is to re-establish a closed globe immediately so that intraocular contents are not expelled. Option C bundles the correct immediate manoeuvres: fill the chamber with viscoelastic and apply digital pressure while the suture is being handed over, then close the wound. Continuing phacoemulsification invites expulsion of lens and vitreous, and injecting BSS cannot counteract the rising suprachoroidal pressure. Posterior sclerotomies may be considered, but only after the wound is secure, and their timing and value remain debated.

Iris melanomas carry the best prognosis among uveal melanomas, with metastatic mortality of roughly 5 to 15 percent, because they are visible early and therefore small at detection, are more often spindle cell type, and less frequently carry monosomy 3. Ciliary body melanomas fare worst because they grow silently behind the iris and present late with large tumour volume. Choroidal melanoma sits in between, with prognosis driven mainly by tumour size and cytogenetics. Conjunctival melanoma is not a uveal melanoma at all, and its mortality of roughly 25 percent exceeds that of iris melanoma, so it is not the answer.

In an eye with chronic HLA-B27 uveitis the goals are maximum uveal biocompatibility and secure in-the-bag fixation away from uveal tissue, and a one-piece hydrophobic acrylic lens has the lowest rate of giant cell deposits and posterior synechiae of the options offered. Polypropylene (Prolene) haptics enhance leucocyte adhesion and should be avoided in uveitic eyes. An unmodified PMMA optic attracts more cellular deposits than acrylic, and the option deliberately excludes the heparin surface modification that would mitigate this. An open-loop anterior chamber lens is the worst choice, since chronic iris and angle contact in an already inflamed eye risks flaring the uveitis, UGH syndrome, glaucoma and endothelial decompensation.

Infectious crystalline keratopathy classically appears in a chronically steroid-treated graft as white, branching, needle-like or fernlike stromal opacities with strikingly little surrounding inflammation, and the organism recovered in the majority of cases is viridans group streptococcus. The indolent, non-inflamed picture reflects organisms growing in a biofilm within the stromal lamellae, which shields them from both the host response and topical antibiotics, and topical corticosteroid further blunts the reaction. Staphylococcal species, other streptococci, Haemophilus and even Candida can produce an identical appearance but are considerably less common. Treatment is fortified topical antibiotics such as vancomycin with tapering of the corticosteroid, and repeat keratoplasty in refractory cases.

BCSC gives the superonasal quadrant just posterior to the limbus as the commonest site of scleral rupture after blunt trauma, because the sclera is relatively thin there and most blunt objects strike the globe from the inferotemporal side, producing rupture in the quadrant opposite the impact. Ruptures characteristically run in a circumferential arc parallel to the limbus, and other weak points are just behind the rectus muscle insertions and at the equator. In a previously operated eye the old cataract or keratoplasty wound is the weakest point and gives way first, which is why surgical history matters when you suspect occult rupture.

This is the same suprachoroidal haemorrhage or effusion scenario as the earlier item, and the first action once it is recognised is to close the incision, by suture or by digital pressure, to re-establish a closed globe and prevent expulsion of intraocular contents. Continuing surgery risks losing the lens and vitreous, and injecting BSS cannot counteract the rising posterior pressure. Posterior sclerotomies may be considered afterwards to drain suprachoroidal blood, decompress the globe and allow reposition of prolapsed tissue, but only once the wound is secure.

Given these three choices the limbus is the best answer, since the classic teaching is that blunt-trauma rupture in a phakic eye occurs in a circumferential arc near the limbus, most often superonasally. Option A is wrong as written because ruptures at the rectus insertions run circumferentially, parallel to the limbus, rather than radially. Option C is a bare negation rather than an anatomical site and cannot be the intended key.
concern: The item conflates two different facts. The sclera is anatomically thinnest, roughly 0.3 mm, immediately behind the rectus muscle insertions, whereas the commonest clinical site of rupture after blunt trauma is the superonasal limbal region. If the examiner meant thinnest literally, the correct answer would be behind the rectus insertions, as the source note itself concedes. B is defensible only because the muscle-insertion option specifies a radial orientation, which is incorrect.

explanation: Mooren ulcer begins as a peripheral crescentic infiltrate within the interpalpebral fissure and advances with a characteristic undermined, overhanging leading edge, leaving a thinned, vascularised bed behind, so the direction of advance that defines the disease is centrally across the cornea. Sparing of the sclera is a cardinal feature and is precisely what separates Mooren ulcer from the peripheral ulcerative keratitis of systemic vasculitis such as granulomatosis with polyangiitis or rheumatoid arthritis, so extension toward the sclera is wrong. Perforation, when it happens, occurs through the thinned central bed rather than at the limbus.
concern: BCSC describes Mooren ulcer as spreading circumferentially and then centrally, so option C is also a true statement about its behaviour and the recall does not make clear which the examiner intended. Central spread with an undermined edge is the more emblematic feature, so A is defensible, but the item is genuinely ambiguous between A and C.

explanation: A shallow anterior chamber after cataract surgery is classified by the intraocular pressure, so measuring the pressure is the single step that most narrows the differential. A shallow chamber with low pressure points to a wound leak or a serous choroidal effusion, whereas a shallow chamber with high pressure points to pupillary block, aqueous misdirection or suprachoroidal haemorrhage, and these two groups have opposite treatments. Ultrasound is valuable afterwards, once the pressure has told you whether to look for a suprachoroidal collection, and pachymetry and gonioscopy do not resolve the diagnosis in a painful, diffusely shallow chamber. Absence of hypopyon makes endophthalmitis less likely but does not exclude it, so the eye still needs close review.

A posterior subcapsular cataract sits immediately in front of the nodal point, directly on the visual axis, so symptoms are worst when the pupil constricts and the opacity occupies proportionally more of the aperture. That is why glare and haloes in bright sunlight or against oncoming headlights are the complaint patients volunteer most, and why acuity in a dim examination lane can be far better than the patient's real-world function. Near vision is also characteristically reduced more than distance vision, because accommodative miosis brings the opacity fully across the pupil, so both listed symptoms are genuine; glare is the classic single best answer because it is the symptom disproportionate to the measured Snellen acuity.

Cement contains calcium hydroxide, or lime, a strong alkali, and alkaline injuries are the most damaging chemical ocular injuries because the hydroxide ion saponifies the fatty acids of cell membranes while the cation penetrates rapidly through cornea into the anterior chamber, causing limbal stem cell loss, deep stromal damage and secondary glaucoma. Cement is additionally dangerous because gritty particles lodge in the fornices and keep releasing alkali until removed, so double lid eversion and sweeping after copious irrigation are mandatory. Household bleach, sodium hypochlorite, is intensely irritating but relatively superficial in its effect. Battery fluid is sulphuric acid, and acids coagulate surface proteins, which limits deeper penetration, so an acid burn generally does less long-term damage than a comparable alkali burn.

Conjunctival lymphoma is overwhelmingly a low-grade extranodal marginal zone (MALT) lymphoma, and disease confined to the conjunctiva is highly radiosensitive, so low-dose or ultra-low-dose external beam radiotherapy is usually curative and is the standard local treatment. Systemic chemotherapy is reserved for systemic or high-grade disease, and rituximab, intralesional interferon alfa-2b, cryotherapy and in some centres antibiotic therapy directed at Chlamydia psittaci are other options. Every patient still needs biopsy for histological and immunophenotypic diagnosis plus systemic staging, because a substantial minority, quoted up to about a third, have or subsequently develop systemic lymphoma.

The OCT shows pseudophakic cystoid macular oedema, Irvine-Gass syndrome, which classically appears about 4 to 12 weeks after surgery and is far more likely after a complicated case with vitreous loss. The mechanism is surgical inflammation with prostaglandin-mediated breakdown of the blood-retinal barrier, which is exactly why topical NSAID plus corticosteroid is first-line treatment. Vitreomacular traction can follow vitreous loss and can cause oedema, but the OCT would show a taut hyaloid tenting the fovea, which is absent. Weak intercellular adhesions describes the schisis cavities of X-linked retinoschisis, and ischaemia-driven VEGF release describes diabetic or vein-occlusion oedema, and neither fits an eye with no other ocular history.

Venous beading and retinal neovascularisation are the two findings that indicate genuine widespread capillary non-perfusion, and neovascularisation in particular means enough ischaemia to drive VEGF release, so option B is the only pair in which both features are unequivocal ischaemic markers. Microaneurysms and hard exudates reflect leakage from an incompetent but still perfused capillary bed rather than ischaemia, which eliminates A and D. IRMA is a true ischaemic sign, but pairing it with microaneurysms or with blot haemorrhages, both of which occur in purely exudative hypertensive change, makes A and C less specific than B.

Uveal effusion syndrome occurs in nanophthalmic or highly hyperopic eyes whose thickened, abnormal sclera obstructs vortex vein outflow and impedes transscleral egress of protein, producing a shifting exudative retinal detachment. Chronic RPE change then gives the characteristic leopard-spot pattern of alternating hypo- and hyperfluorescence, and the crucial detail is that there is no leakage, which excludes an inflammatory or neovascular cause. BDUMP also produces leopard spotting and is associated with an occult systemic carcinoma, but a family history rather than a personal history of lung cancer is a deliberate red herring, and the +6.00 refraction points firmly to uveal effusion. CAR causes photoreceptor dysfunction with an extinguished ERG rather than an exudative detachment, and multiple sclerosis is unrelated.

Bacillus species, especially Bacillus cereus, are the organisms classically associated with endophthalmitis in intravenous drug users, and also with endophthalmitis after soil-contaminated penetrating trauma. The presentation is fulminant, evolving over hours with severe pain, fever, a ring corneal infiltrate and profound vision loss, and it demands immediate intravitreal antibiotics including vancomycin, with early vitrectomy considered. Streptococci are the commonest cause of endogenous bacterial endophthalmitis overall in North America but usually arise from endocarditis, Staphylococcus aureus typically from a skin or soft tissue focus, and enterococcus is uncommon. Candida is the other organism to remember in this population and can coexist in the differential.

Duration of diabetes is the single strongest predictor of both the presence and the severity of diabetic retinopathy, as the WESDR data showed, with nearly all type 1 patients having some retinopathy after 20 years of disease. Glycaemic control, established by the DCCT and UKPDS, is the most important modifiable risk factor and is what you actually intervene on, but it is not the strongest determinant of who develops retinopathy. Hypertension and hyperlipidaemia are additional modifiable contributors, hypertension particularly to progression and hyperlipidaemia particularly to hard exudate and maculopathy, but both rank below duration and glycaemic control.

Longer wavelengths are absorbed much less by haemoglobin, so krypton red at 647 nm passes through a blood-tinged media that would absorb blue-green light, allowing panretinal photocoagulation to be delivered despite vitreous or preretinal haemorrhage. Argon blue-green is strongly absorbed by both haemoglobin and macular xanthophyll, so it is ineffective through blood and hazardous near the fovea. Yellow dye laser at 577 nm is well absorbed by oxyhaemoglobin, which is exactly what you want for treating vascular lesions and exactly what you do not want when trying to shoot past blood. In modern practice an 810 nm diode serves the same role as krypton red for this indication.

Bleb-associated endophthalmitis is dominated by streptococci, which appear on Gram stain as gram-positive cocci in chains, because a thin, avascular, often microscopically leaking bleb gives ocular surface flora direct access to the eye. Haemophilus influenzae, a gram-negative coccobacillus, is the other characteristic organism and is why option A appears, but streptococci are the more frequent finding when both are offered. The virulence of these organisms explains the abrupt, painful presentation and the notoriously poor visual prognosis of blebitis progressing to endophthalmitis, in sharp contrast to the indolent coagulase-negative staphylococcal infection typical after cataract surgery.

This is the Wright question in which the option list deliberately omits gram-positive cocci in chains, so among the choices offered gram-negative coccobacilli, meaning Haemophilus influenzae, is the expected answer for bleb-associated endophthalmitis. Streptococcus and H. influenzae are the two organisms characteristically responsible, entering through a thin, leaking or even apparently intact filtering bleb, and they account for the abrupt onset and poor prognosis. Gram-positive cocci in clusters would be staphylococci, more typical of the delayed indolent postcataract infection; gram-positive rods suggest Bacillus or Cutibacterium; and branching pseudohyphae would be fungal, which is rare in bleb-related disease.

A cilioretinal artery, present in roughly 15 to 30 percent of eyes, arises from the short posterior ciliary circulation, usually via the peripapillary choroid or the circle of Zinn-Haller, rather than from the central retinal artery. That separate origin is precisely why it stays perfused during a central retinal artery occlusion and can preserve central acuity, which matches the described fundus whitening with a spared foveal island and the angiogram showing filling of only those few vessels. The central retinal artery, the posterior ciliary arteries and the lacrimal artery are all branches of the ophthalmic artery, so answering ophthalmic artery is one step too proximal for a question asking which vessel the cilioretinal artery most directly branches from.

The Optic Neuritis Treatment Trial established that the number of demyelinating white matter lesions on brain MRI at presentation is the strongest predictor of conversion to multiple sclerosis: about 22 percent at 10 years with no lesions versus about 56 percent with one or more, against an overall 10-year risk near 38 percent. That is why brain MRI is obtained in every case of typical optic neuritis, and it is now also the basis for deciding on disease-modifying therapy. Orbital MRI may show enhancement of the affected nerve but only confirms a diagnosis that is already clinical and carries no prognostic weight. Family history modifies risk only slightly and non-quantitatively, and subclinical contralateral field defects, though common, do not predict conversion.

Cocaine 10% blocks reuptake of noradrenaline at the iris dilator, so a normally innervated pupil dilates while an oculosympathetically denervated Horner pupil does not, whatever the level of the lesion. Because the magnitude of a normal eye's response varies between individuals, the test is standardised by instilling drops in both eyes and comparing them, and a post-cocaine anisocoria of about 1 mm or more, with 0.8 mm often quoted, confirms Horner syndrome. Options A and B are wrong because instilling in one eye only removes the internal control, and absolute dilation of a single eye is not a reliable criterion. Reversal of anisocoria in option C is the endpoint of the apraclonidine test, which exploits denervation supersensitivity of the dilator, not the cocaine test.

Rifampin and the other rifamycins are excreted in body fluids and turn urine, sweat, saliva and tears orange-red, which is harmless but permanently stains soft contact lenses, so patients must be warned in advance. Isoniazid and ethambutol are the antituberculous drugs to fear ophthalmically because both cause toxic optic neuropathy, ethambutol classically dose- and duration-related with central scotomas, reduced acuity and red-green dyschromatopsia, requiring baseline and interval visual monitoring. Pyrazinamide causes hepatotoxicity, hyperuricaemia and polyarthralgia rather than any distinctive ocular sign.

Whenever an anterior chamber intraocular lens is placed, a patent iridectomy is required to prevent pupillary block, and it should be made surgically at the time of the operation, because a laser iridotomy in an eye that has just had vitreous prolapse is very likely to be plugged by residual vitreous strands. BCSC places this surgical iridectomy superiorly, at 12 o'clock, where it lies beneath the upper lid and is less likely to produce dysphotopsia. The inferior 6 o'clock position is reserved for eyes that will contain something buoyant, namely an air or gas bubble after endothelial keratoplasty or silicone oil after retinal detachment repair, because a bubble floats up and occludes a superior iridectomy. Option B is unsafe, and options C and D defer to a laser procedure that may well close.

Recurrent oral ulceration, genital ulceration presenting as dysuria, a hypopyon uveitis with intense injection, and an occlusive retinal vasculitis with vitritis and macular oedema is Behcet disease, associated with HLA-B51 and classically prevalent along the historical Silk Road. The hypopyon of Behcet is characteristically mobile and shifts with head position, and the sight-threatening element is the posterior occlusive vasculitis, which requires systemic immunosuppression rather than corticosteroid alone. HLA-A29 is birdshot chorioretinopathy, HLA-DR2 or DR15 is linked to pars planitis, and HLA-B27 underlies the acute recurrent unilateral anterior uveitis of the spondyloarthropathies, which is the main mimic here because it too can form a hypopyon, but it does not produce retinal vasculitis or oral and genital ulceration.

Rifampin colours urine, sweat, saliva and tears orange-red because the drug and its metabolites are excreted in body fluids, and the reaction is harmless, needing only reassurance and a warning about permanent staining of soft contact lenses. Streptomycin causes vestibulocochlear toxicity and nephrotoxicity, ethambutol causes a dose-related toxic optic neuropathy with reduced acuity and dyschromatopsia, and pyrazinamide causes hepatotoxicity and hyperuricaemia. None of the other three discolours secretions, so the history alone identifies the drug.

The snowbank of pars planitis is an organised fibrovascular and fibroglial membrane overlying the pars plana and peripheral retina, containing new vessels, condensed vitreous collagen, fibrous astrocytes and Muller cell processes with scattered mononuclear leucocytes. Its vascularity matters clinically because it explains why these eyes can develop vitreous haemorrhage and tractional detachment, particularly in children. Multinucleated giant cells are the hallmark of granulomatous inflammation such as sarcoidosis and are not what constitutes a snowbank, so B is wrong. Macular oedema is the commonest cause of vision loss in pars planitis but is a separate finding, not the content of the snowbank.

The photograph shows large, greasy, mutton-fat keratic precipitates on the inferior corneal endothelium, the granulomatous pattern expected in a young Black patient with hilar lymphadenopathy and therefore sarcoidosis. Mutton-fat precipitates are large precisely because they consist of bulky mononuclear phagocytes, that is macrophages and the epithelioid cells they differentiate into, sometimes with multinucleated giant cells. Non-granulomatous precipitates are small and fine and are composed of lymphocytes and neutrophils, which is why lymphocytes and PMNs are wrong, and fine fibrin deposits give the small dot precipitates seen in HLA-B27 disease.
concern: Options A and C are not truly separable, since epithelioid cells are transformed macrophages and standard texts describe mutton-fat KPs as containing both. The item would be sound only if one of them were removed; macrophages is the choice usually keyed, so the source answer is defensible.

explanation: Histopathology of the snowbank shows a fibrovascular and fibroglial membrane: proliferating glial tissue with fibrous astrocytes and condensed vitreous collagen, together with new blood vessels, and lymphocytic cuffing of the adjacent peripheral retinal veins with a predominance of T helper cells. The fibrovascular component is the answer because it accounts for the risk of vitreous haemorrhage and traction in these eyes. Lipid exudate would point to Coats disease or another exudative retinopathy, and accumulation of epithelioid histiocytes describes granuloma formation, which would suggest sarcoidosis rather than idiopathic pars planitis.

Elevated intraocular pressure during active anterior uveitis is the finding that should make you think of herpetic disease, because herpesviruses cause a trabeculitis that raises pressure at a time when most other uveitides lower it through ciliary body hyposecretion; pressures of 40 to 60 mm Hg are described, and inflammatory cells add further outflow obstruction. The supporting features of herpetic anterior uveitis are unilaterality, sectoral or patchy iris atrophy with a distorted pupil, reduced corneal sensation, and past or concurrent keratitis, and treatment requires antiviral cover alongside steroid. Stellate keratic precipitates do occur in herpetic and especially CMV anterior uveitis, but they are equally or more characteristic of Fuchs heterochromic uveitis, so they are the weaker discriminator here.
concern: I would answer B. BCSC Uveitis states that ocular hypertension associated with herpetic uveitis may be a helpful diagnostic hallmark, and in the same passage that diffuse or stellate KPs are not pathognomonic of any particular condition. The source explanation quotes both of those sentences yet keys A, so the explanation argues against its own answer. Raised IOP from trabeculitis is the classic teaching point for herpetic anterior uveitis, while stellate KPs are most strongly linked to Fuchs heterochromic uveitis and CMV anterior uveitis. This looks like a transcription error in the answer key rather than a genuine difference of opinion.

explanation: Apraclonidine causes allergic follicular conjunctivitis and periocular contact dermatitis in roughly 20 to 40 percent of patients on chronic therapy, by far the highest rate among the drugs listed, and that is exactly why its use is now confined to short-term blunting of pressure spikes around laser and cataract surgery. Brimonidine, a more selective alpha-2 agonist, causes the same reaction considerably less often and later, and less still with the purite-preserved lower concentrations. Dorzolamide typically causes stinging and a bitter taste, with sulfonamide hypersensitivity as its important allergy, and latanoprost causes conjunctival hyperaemia, lash growth and iris and periocular pigmentation rather than the itchy allergic dermatitis described.

A subluxed lens plugging the pupil produces pupillary block, and the office treatment is laser iridotomy, but in ectopia lentis BCSC recommends two iridotomies placed 180 degrees apart, because a mobile lens can shift and occlude a single opening whereas it cannot cover two diametrically opposed openings simultaneously. Placing them only 90 degrees apart leaves both within reach of the same displaced lens. A single iridotomy, superior or inferior, is the standard for ordinary phakic pupillary block but is unreliable when the blocking element is mobile. Definitive management once the acute block is broken is lens extraction.

After only one week of prednisolone this pressure rise is almost certainly not a steroid response, which typically takes two to six weeks, and the persisting 2+ cell tells you the inflammation is undertreated and that the trabecular meshwork is obstructed by inflammatory cells and debris. The correct move is therefore to intensify rather than reduce the corticosteroid and to add a pressure-lowering agent, and brimonidine is a good choice because it lowers pressure without any pro-inflammatory effect. Prostaglandin analogues are relatively contraindicated in active uveitis because of concern about worsening inflammation and cystoid macular oedema, excluding B, and pilocarpine is contraindicated because it increases vascular permeability and promotes posterior synechiae, excluding C. Options A and B are additionally wrong because they taper steroid while inflammation is still active.

An elderly eye with a hypermature cataract, an acutely painful pressure of 48 mm Hg, marked cell and flare but no keratic precipitates, and a widely open angle at Shaffer grade III, is phacolytic glaucoma: high-molecular-weight lens protein leaks through an intact but microscopically permeable capsule and, with the swollen macrophages that engulf it, obstructs an anatomically open trabecular meshwork. Phacomorphic glaucoma is excluded by the open angle, since it is an angle closure driven by an intumescent lens. Lens particle glaucoma requires a capsular breach from trauma or surgery, which is absent. Phacoantigenic glaucoma is a granulomatous reaction to lens protein after capsular disruption and characteristically shows keratic precipitates, which the stem specifically says are absent. Definitive treatment is cataract extraction once the pressure is medically controlled.

A cyclodialysis cleft is a disinsertion of the ciliary body from the scleral spur and is a classic sequel of blunt trauma with hyphaema; the direct route it creates from anterior chamber into the suprachoroidal space, combined with reduced aqueous production, produces prolonged profound hypotony such as the pressure of 4 mm Hg described. The diagnostically decisive event is spontaneous closure of the cleft, which abruptly restores aqueous production against an outflow system that has been suppressed and is often also damaged, causing a sudden marked pressure spike with pain and headache. Angle recession glaucoma does raise pressure after trauma, but it does so insidiously months to years later and does not explain the preceding months of hypotony. Gonioscopy or ultrasound biomicroscopy confirms the cleft.

Radial, spoke-like mid-peripheral iris transillumination defects with symptoms triggered by exercise are pigment dispersion syndrome: a posteriorly bowed peripheral iris chafes against the anterior zonular packets, releasing melanin granules that shower the anterior segment during vigorous exercise or pupillary dilation and transiently clog the trabecular meshwork. The typical patient is a young myopic adult, and the pressure between episodes may be entirely normal, exactly as described. Supporting signs are a Krukenberg spindle on the endothelium, a deep chamber with a concave peripheral iris, and a dense homogeneous trabecular pigment band. Pseudoexfoliation occurs in an older population and produces peripupillary, moth-eaten transillumination with white flaky material at the pupil margin and on the anterior lens capsule.

Hypotony maculopathy after trabeculectomy is driven by patient factors rather than by the glaucoma subtype itself, and the two strongest risk factors are young age and myopia, because a thin, distensible young myopic sclera folds inward and the choroid thickens when pressure falls. Pigmentary glaucoma is the entity on this list whose typical patient is precisely a young myopic adult, so it carries the highest risk. Pseudoexfoliative glaucoma occurs in elderly, often hyperopic patients with rigid sclera, and steroid-induced and angle-recession glaucoma carry no such association. Practically this means tighter or releasable scleral flap sutures and more cautious antimetabolite dosing in these eyes.

Mid-peripheral, radial spoke-like iris transillumination defects are essentially diagnostic of pigment dispersion syndrome, produced by the posteriorly bowed peripheral iris rubbing against the anterior zonules. The history of blurred vision after exercise fits perfectly: exertion liberates a shower of pigment that transiently obstructs the trabecular meshwork, spiking the pressure and producing corneal oedema with haloes, blurring and ache. Pseudoexfoliation gives a different picture, with peripupillary moth-eaten transillumination in an older patient plus white flaky material at the pupil margin and on the anterior lens capsule, and its pressure rises are not exercise-related.

Hypotony maculopathy is the complication for which young age and myopia are the established risk factors, because a thin, elastic sclera collapses inward when pressure falls after a filtering procedure, producing chorioretinal folds and reduced acuity; the risk is amplified by antimetabolites such as mitomycin C. Aqueous misdirection is instead the risk of the small, crowded, hyperopic or nanophthalmic eye, so it is essentially the opposite refractive profile. Suprachoroidal haemorrhage is associated with older age, arteriosclerosis, anticoagulation, high preoperative pressure and aphakia rather than youthful myopia. Prevention rests on tighter or releasable scleral flap sutures and judicious antimetabolite use.

In Sturge-Weber syndrome glaucoma develops in a large proportion of affected children, quoted up to about 70 percent, and the strongest clinical predictor is involvement of the upper eyelid, that is the V1 dermatome, by the facial port-wine stain, because that distribution accompanies the episcleral haemangioma that raises episcleral venous pressure. Involvement of the forehead alone, without the eyelid, does not carry the same association. There are two mechanisms: an anterior chamber angle dysgenesis presenting in infancy with buphthalmos, and a later-onset form driven by elevated episcleral venous pressure. Associated choroidal haemangioma, iris heterochromia and dilated episcleral vessels all further increase the risk.

Apraclonidine has the highest rate of allergic follicular conjunctivitis and periocular contact dermatitis of the topical glaucoma drugs, of the order of 20 to 40 percent with chronic use, which is why it is now restricted to short-term perioperative pressure control rather than long-term therapy. A patient on the same drop for three years complaining of itchy, red eyes and lids is describing exactly this reaction. Brimonidine, a more selective alpha-2 agonist, causes the same allergy far less frequently and typically later in the course, so it is the wrong answer here.
concern: Options A and B name the same drug, since Alphagan is the trade name of brimonidine 0.2 percent, so the item is internally flawed. The flaw does not affect the intended key, which remains apraclonidine.

explanation: Apraclonidine causes allergic follicular conjunctivitis and periocular contact dermatitis in roughly 20 to 40 percent of patients on long-term therapy, the highest rate of the drugs listed, and this loss of effect and tolerability is why it is now used only short-term around laser and cataract surgery. Brimonidine, a more selective alpha-2 agonist, produces the same reaction much less often. Dorzolamide characteristically causes stinging and a bitter taste, with sulfonamide hypersensitivity as its notable allergy, and latanoprost causes hyperaemia, lash growth and pigmentary change rather than an itchy allergic dermatitis, so none of them fits a patient on years of the same drop with itchy red eyes.

In neovascular glaucoma the objective is to remove the ischaemic drive, and panretinal photocoagulation is the definitive treatment; BCSC states that even with 360 degrees of synechial angle closure, PRP should still be performed, because eliminating the angiogenic stimulus reduces the risk of intraoperative bleeding and improves the success of any subsequent tube shunt or trabeculectomy. Anti-VEGF injection is a valuable adjunct that regresses new vessels rapidly and buys time but does not replace retinal ablation. Cyclodestruction, transscleral or endoscopic, is generally reserved for eyes with poor visual potential or pressure that cannot be controlled otherwise, and retrobulbar alcohol is purely for pain relief in a blind, painful eye.
concern: The recall is heavily abbreviated and the options are not reliably legible. The abbreviation hm could mean hand-motion vision or vitreous haemorrhage, and Cbc and through-scleral PRP most likely mean cyclophotocoagulation and transscleral cyclophotocoagulation, as the transcriber themselves suspected. If the stem really describes a dense long-standing vitreous haemorrhage obscuring the fundus, conventional slit-lamp PRP may not be deliverable and vitrectomy with endolaser, or transscleral retinal photocoagulation, would be the practical route. The underlying principle that ablating ischaemic retina is the definitive treatment still favours B.

explanation: Goldmann applanation assumes a cornea of roughly average thickness and normal biomechanics; oedema makes the cornea more compliant and easier to flatten, so the reading is falsely low, and that is the trap in a decompensated or acutely hypertensive eye whose true pressure is higher than measured. A corneal scar is denser and more rigid and gives falsely high readings, as does increased scleral rigidity with indentation (Schiotz) tonometry. In such eyes a dynamic contour tonometer, pneumotonometer or Tono-Pen at the corneal periphery gives a more trustworthy figure.
concern: Options A and D overlap, since stromal oedema is a form of corneal oedema and points in the same direction. D is the general textbook statement and is the intended key, but the item would be cleaner with only one of the two offered.

explanation: Reversal of optic disc cupping after successful pressure lowering is well documented in infants and young children and is one of the most useful signs that surgery for congenital glaucoma has worked; it occurs because the immature, elastic lamina cribrosa and peripapillary sclera can spring back once pressure is normalised. In adults, by contrast, glaucomatous cupping is essentially irreversible, which is why this finding is specific to the paediatric setting. Progression of cupping in this child would signal uncontrolled pressure and a failed procedure. The other markers of successful control at this age are stabilisation of axial length and corneal diameter and clearing of corneal oedema and Haab striae.

The oculocardiac reflex, in which traction on an extraocular muscle produces bradycardia or even asystole via the ciliary nerves to the ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve and then to the vagal nucleus, is most often provoked by traction on the medial rectus, the muscle most frequently and most forcibly engaged in strabismus surgery. The immediate response is to release the traction, which usually aborts the bradycardia, with intravenous atropine or glycopyrrolate if it recurs or is severe, and adequate depth of anaesthesia reduces the incidence. Any muscle can trigger the reflex and children are the most susceptible, but the medial rectus is the expected answer.

This is infantile esotropia: onset before 6 months of age, a large and stable angle of 50 prism dioptres, a refraction that is physiological for an infant so the deviation is non-accommodative, and free alternation indicating no amblyopia. A deviation of this size presenting in this window will not resolve spontaneously, and waiting until age 2 forfeits the chance to develop any binocular function, so surgical alignment at around 6 to 12 months is the accepted management. Alternate patching treats or prevents amblyopia, which this child does not have, and does not straighten the eyes. Prism of the magnitude needed for 50 prism dioptres is optically impractical in spectacles, and a +1.00 correction would not reduce a non-accommodative deviation.

The diagnostic key is the mismatch between full ductions when one eye is covered and an apparent bilateral abduction deficit on versions, which localises the problem to excess convergence rather than to a sixth nerve palsy. Add miosis and pseudomyopia of -3.00 that would disappear on cycloplegia, and the triad of excessive convergence, accommodation and miosis defines spasm of the near reflex, in a setting, an anxious student in finals week, that fits its usual functional aetiology. Divergence insufficiency causes esotropia greater at distance than at near with normal pupils, accommodative insufficiency causes blurred near vision rather than esotropia and miosis, and Horner syndrome gives a miotic pupil with ptosis but no esotropia and no abduction limitation. Treatment is reassurance, addressing the stressor, and cycloplegia, sometimes with a bifocal add.

Angle kappa is the angle between the visual axis and the pupillary axis. A negative angle kappa displaces the corneal light reflex temporally in each eye, making the eyes look as though they are turned inward, so it simulates esotropia, that is pseudoesotropia. A positive angle kappa, the commoner situation, displaces the reflex nasally and simulates exotropia, and it is why children with temporally dragged maculae, as in retinopathy of prematurity, look exotropic. In either case the distinguishing test is the cover test, which shows no refixation movement in pseudostrabismus, and epicanthal folds with a broad nasal bridge are the other common cause of an esotropic appearance in infants.

Bilateral abduction deficit with limited adduction and, crucially, a face that has never smiled points to Mobius syndrome, in which both the sixth and seventh cranial nerve nuclei are affected, producing a masklike face, incomplete lid closure, feeding difficulty, and often a full horizontal gaze palsy when the paramedian pontine reticular formation is also involved. Associated limb, chest wall and tongue anomalies are common, and exposure keratopathy is the main ophthalmic hazard to manage. Duane syndrome type 3 also limits both abduction and adduction, but it is usually unilateral, shows globe retraction with palpebral fissure narrowing on adduction, and involves no facial nerve deficit, so it cannot explain the absent smile.

Marcus Gunn jaw-winking is a congenital cranial dysinnervation disorder in which fibres of the motor division of the trigeminal nerve, cranial nerve V, destined for the pterygoid muscles are miswired to the levator palpebrae superioris, so the ptotic lid elevates when the jaw moves laterally or when an infant sucks. Cranial nerve VII is the answer to a different phenomenon, aberrant regeneration after facial palsy, which produces synkinetic lid closure on smiling and crocodile tears, and cranial nerve VIII has no motor supply to lid or jaw. Note that the underlying miswiring is trigeminal to oculomotor, so describing this as aberrant regeneration of the third nerve is loose language; true aberrant third nerve regeneration causes lid elevation on adduction or downgaze after an acquired third nerve palsy.
